# Decoupling Brake and Running Lights in a Jeep WJ

You've replaced a bulb, and suddenly your brake lights work perfectly, but the running lights have vanished. This is a classic symptom of an electrical state change rather than a simple component failure. In a 2001 Jeep Wrangler (WJ) with a 4.0L engine, the fuse box appears normal, yet the circuit behaves as if it has lost its "always-on" power source while retaining its switched ground or activation path.

The core issue lies in how the lighting circuit is wired on this platform. The running lights and brake lights share the same bulb socket; they are not independent circuits powered by separate fuses. Instead, the system relies on a relay logic where the running lights require constant power (battery live), while the brake lights receive that constant power plus an additional signal from the brake pedal switch to illuminate brighter.

When you swapped the bulb, it is highly probable that you inadvertently disconnected or damaged the harness tab responsible for the running light feed, or perhaps moved a clip back into a position where it only contacts the brake circuit. Alternatively, if the vehicle has aftermarket wiring modifications, the relay controlling the constant power might have been bypassed during installation of the new bulb.

To diagnose this systematically without pulling every fuse, you need to understand the specific fuse assignments for the WJ generation. The lighting logic is split between two primary fuses in the under-dash panel: the "DOME" and "RUNNING LIGHTS" circuits often share a designation or are tied together, while the brake activation is handled separately via the stop lamp relay.

If your dashboard illumination works but the external running lights do not, check the 15-amp fuse labeled "Running Lights" (often found in the passenger side under-dash box). However, since the bulb physically works for braking, the filament is intact. The failure is almost certainly a loss of power at the socket's constant feed pin.

Use a multimeter to probe the back of the bulb socket with the ignition off but the key in the "ON" position (or simply check the battery terminal continuity if you have a test light). You are looking for 12V on the specific contact that feeds the running light side of the dual-filament bulb. If there is no voltage here, trace back to the relay. On many WJ models, the "Running Lights" function is controlled by a specific relay located in the engine bay fuse box near the firewall.

If you suspect a loose connection at the headlight assembly—a common occurrence after vibration over 23 years—disconnect the main connector and check for corrosion or broken pins. The fact that brake lights work confirms the ground side of the circuit is fine; the issue is isolated to the hot wire path.

In rare cases involving aftermarket modules, a software reset via OBD-II might be required if an integration module was disturbed during bulb replacement. However, given the age and mechanical nature of the WJ wiring harness, physical disconnection is the most likely culprit. If you are comfortable opening the headlight buckets to inspect the socket contacts directly, do so before assuming a fuse failure, as blown fuses rarely cause this specific split behavior without affecting other circuits sharing the same line.
